projects.title: DailyFX
projects.subtitle: Trading platform redesign · IG Group · 2014–2020
projects.description: A complete redesign of the DailyFX trading analysis platform, improving UX for both novice and expert traders through better data visualization, streamlined information architecture, and a cohesive design system built for scale.
projects.tension: How do you build for scale when a wrong component costs someone real money?

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: A complete redesign of the DailyFX trading analysis platform — the world's most-visited forex news and analysis portal. The goal was to make dense, data-heavy content accessible to both first-time retail traders and seasoned professionals, without stripping the depth that experts rely on.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: DailyFX had accumulated years of feature additions without a coherent information architecture. Key problems: content was buried under layers of navigation, charts and editorial competed for the same visual space, and the design system was fragmented across markets and locales. The redesign had to work across 10+ languages and serve a global audience with radically different trading contexts.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: I led end-to-end redesign: from IA restructure and component audit through to building a shared design system used across IG's global product suite. I ran design sprints with editorial, engineering, and data teams to align on priorities, then shipped in iterative phases to avoid disruption to the existing audience.

projects.title: Brainly Tutoring
projects.subtitle: Live EdTech · Mobile-first · 0 to 1
projects.description: Designed the end-to-end experience for Brainly's live tutoring feature, enabling millions of students to connect with expert tutors in real-time. Led research, prototyping, and cross-functional delivery from 0 to 1.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Designed the end-to-end experience for Brainly's live tutoring feature — from matching a student to a tutor through to the live session and post-session review. This was a zero-to-one product built alongside a cross-functional team of engineers, product managers, and data scientists.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Brainly's core model was asynchronous — post a question, wait for a community answer. Live tutoring was a fundamentally different product loop: real-time, high-stakes, and requiring trust signals that asynchronous interaction had never needed. The biggest design challenge was building confidence fast, for both the student and the tutor.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: I ran discovery with students and tutors across four markets, synthesised findings into clear design principles, then moved quickly into prototyping. I worked closely with mobile engineers throughout — designing components to match the iOS and Android constraints, not fighting against them.

projects.title: Storebox
projects.subtitle: First digital self-storage in Europe · Consumer app
projects.description: Led product design at Storebox — Europe's first fully digital self-storage solution. Designed the complete customer journey from discovery to booking to smart-lock access management, replacing all physical touchpoints.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Led product design at Storebox — Europe's first fully digital self-storage solution. The brief was to replace every physical touchpoint in the storage journey with a seamless digital experience: find a unit, book it, pay, and access it via smart lock — all without human interaction.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: I owned the complete customer journey — from the marketing site through to the app used to open the storage unit. This meant designing across three surfaces (web, iOS, Android) with a consistent interaction model, and working closely with hardware engineers to design interfaces for the smart lock access flow.

projects.title: PandaDoc CPQ Rules Engine for HubSpot
projects.subtitle: Guided selling for reps, full expressiveness for sales ops
projects.description: The rules engine had to carry the accumulated expertise of sales ops, finance, and legal — silently, so the rep never had to think about it.
projects.tension: A sales rep needs to generate an accurate quote in minutes, sometimes mid-call. But the pricing logic behind that quote — volume discounts, approval thresholds, automatic add-ons — is the accumulated expertise of sales ops, finance, and legal. The rep who gets it wrong sends a number the company can't honour. The rep who has to stop and ask someone gets it right but loses the deal. The rules engine had to carry that expertise silently, so the rep never had to think about it.

sections.heading: The tension
sections.body: A sales rep needs to generate an accurate quote fast — sometimes mid-call. But the pricing logic behind that quote is complex: volume discounts, approval thresholds, automatic add-ons, bundle rules. It's the accumulated expertise of sales ops, finance, and legal, built up over years. A rep who gets it wrong sends the customer a number the company can't honour. A rep who has to stop and ask someone gets it right but kills the deal. The standard response to this problem is restriction — lock the fields, block the errors. But that mistakes the problem. The rep isn't trying to do something wrong. They just don't have the pricing expertise of a senior sales manager, and they're being asked to make pricing decisions in real time. The rep doesn't need to be prevented. They need to be guided.

sections.heading: Role and scope
sections.body:
I was the sole designer on this project. I owned the rules engine admin UI, the guided selling playbook flow, and the two-way data sync between PandaDoc and HubSpot. There was no other designer on this work. I worked with a PM and an engineering team, and collaborated directly with HubSpot's partner team on the integration's UX requirements.

What this did not include: the core PandaDoc document editor, the pricing table UI, and the eSignature flow. Those were existing surfaces the CPQ integration connected to, not rebuilt.

sections.heading: The hard problem
sections.body:
A rules engine has two audiences who never see each other's experience. The admin — a sales ops manager — is setting up the system once. They know the pricing logic in depth. They need expressive power: the ability to combine conditions, set actions, define what triggers approval. If the interface is too simplified, they can't represent the business logic accurately and the whole system breaks down.

The sales rep is working inside the system every day. They have no visibility into what rules exist. The rules should be invisible to them — not hidden, but unnecessary to think about. Their job is to sell, not to navigate a configuration interface.

The tension: a rules engine expressive enough for the admin is, by definition, complex. And complexity that leaks into the rep's experience defeats the entire purpose of having the engine in the first place.

sections.text: The admin isn't configuring restrictions. They're encoding the team's collective pricing judgment so it can operate without them in the room.

sections.heading: Natural language framing over technical syntax
sections.body:
Early explorations used a conditional logic builder in the style of a developer tool: dropdowns for field names, operators, values. Technically complete. Practically alienating for a sales ops user who thinks in business terms, not data terms. I argued for framing every rule as a sentence the admin could read aloud and recognise as their own business logic. "When a rep selects [product], automatically apply [discount]." "When manual discount is above [threshold], require approval from [approver]."

The fields were still structured — they had to be, for the engine to process them — but the interface presented them as a plain-language statement being assembled, not a query being written. The trade-off: this constrained expressiveness to what could be represented in readable sentence form. Some edge cases couldn't be expressed this way. I made the call to cover 90% of real use cases with a readable interface rather than build a maximally expressive tool most admins would find intimidating.

sections.caption: Rule builder in action: structured fields presented as a readable sentence rather than a query. The same underlying logic, legible to a sales ops manager without technical training.

sections.heading: The two-way sync as a trust problem
sections.body:
The design challenge of the HubSpot sync was not the data flow — that was an engineering problem. It was how to make the sync legible and trustworthy to the rep. A rep who doesn't understand what data flows where will either distrust the system and duplicate work manually, or trust it blindly and miss sync errors.

I made the sync explicit at the moment it matters rather than invisible by default. When a rep opens a deal in HubSpot and initiates a quote, the interface surfaces a brief readable confirmation of which fields will be pulled. When the quote is completed and sent, a brief confirmation shows what was written back. Not a full data audit — just enough for the rep to know the system did its job.

Legibility and trust are not the same thing. Complete transparency can undermine trust as much as opacity can. The signal I was designing for was trust, not transparency.

sections.caption: Guided selling and the HubSpot two-way sync in action: what comes in from HubSpot when a quote opens, and what writes back after send. The restraint is deliberate — enough to confirm the sync worked, not enough to require the rep to understand it.

sections.heading: Making rules invisible to reps
sections.body:
The playbook is the rep-facing side of the rules engine. The admin builds the rules; the playbook is how those rules manifest as a guided experience when the rep generates a quote. The design principle: it should feel like a checklist, not a configuration interface. The rep follows steps — select product, configure quantities, review pricing — and the rules engine operates silently. Discounts apply automatically. Approvals are triggered. Add-ons appear.

The key design decision was what to surface when the rules produce an output the rep might not expect. A rep who sees a discount appear without understanding why will question the number or try to remove it. A rep told "this quote needs approval" without warning feels the system is working against them. I argued against hiding rule outcomes completely. The direction was to surface them at the moment they occur, in plain language, as confirmations rather than interruptions. "Volume discount applied based on quantity." "This quote will go to your manager for review before sending." Brief, informative, non-blocking. The rep stays in motion.

sections.caption: Inline rule outcome notification in the playbook flow — the moment an approval is triggered. Non-blocking, plain language, in context. The rep knows what happened and why without leaving the flow.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.body:
PandaDoc CPQ for HubSpot launched September 18, 2024, and was presented at INBOUND24 — HubSpot's flagship annual conference. It launched as the first and only fully embedded, native CPQ integration for HubSpot Sales Hub.

Quote error rate decreased. Deal cycle time shortened. Sales rep adoption was faster than previous tooling. PandaDoc was named a HubSpot Essential App for Sales 2024 — the first CPQ integration to receive that recognition. The integration became the foundation for PandaDoc's strategic partnership with HubSpot, a corporate investor in PandaDoc.

sections.caption: Our product manager walks through how the PandaDoc CPQ and HubSpot integration works end to end.

sections.text: With PandaDoc CPQ for HubSpot, we've streamlined our quoting process significantly, allowing us to close deals faster and with greater accuracy, all within the familiar HubSpot environment.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body:
The most useful reframe on this project: rules are not restrictions. They're automation. The instinct in complex systems design is to think about rules as constraints — things that prevent users from doing the wrong thing. That framing produces defensive design. The rules engine in PandaDoc CPQ was about automating the expertise of senior people so that less experienced people could operate at the same quality level without needing to know everything. Not "you can't do that" but "we've already handled that for you." That difference — conceptually small, practically total — shaped every decision in the admin UI.

The second thing: legibility and trust are not the same. A system can be fully transparent and still feel untrustworthy, because the volume of information overwhelms the signal. Trust comes from the right information at the right moment, not from complete information at all times.

projects.title: Brainly Tutor: Live Session Design and India Launch
projects.subtitle: IxD Product Designer — student session experience and India launch
projects.description: A tutor with a desktop, a keyboard, and a whiteboard is not in the same session as a student following along on a five-inch mobile screen — and the gap between those two experiences is exactly where trust breaks down.

sections.body: A tutor with a desktop, a keyboard, and a whiteboard is not in the same session as a student following along on a five-inch mobile screen — and the gap between those two experiences is exactly where trust breaks down.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Brainly Tutor was a live subscription tutoring product built on top of Brainly's existing 350-million-user homework help platform. Students paid $96/year to access on-demand sessions with expert tutors for math and physics. Before this work the session experience was a basic chat interface. The project moved Brainly Tutor from text chat to a full live session — voice and video call, shared whiteboard, LaTeX equation rendering, and screenshare.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: IxD Product Designer — sole designer on the student-facing live session experience. Owned the full session surface: voice/video call, whiteboard interaction on mobile, LaTeX rendering, screenshare. Also owned the India launch: pricing UI, payment flows including the parent payment link feature, onboarding messaging repositioned from homework help to exam preparation, and performance optimisation for low-end Android devices.

sections.caption: Live session interface — voice/video call, shared whiteboard, and LaTeX rendering on student mobile.

sections.heading: Decision 1 — Chat to call
sections.body: Moving from a chat-only session to a call-first experience with whiteboard, LaTeX, and screenshare. The choice was between layering tools onto the existing chat interface vs. replacing it with a call-first session. Call-first was chosen — the product needed to feel categorically different from the free chat-based homework help already on Brainly. Cost accepted: higher friction for students uncomfortable on a live call.

sections.heading: Decision 2 — Whiteboard on mobile
sections.body: Whether the student could draw on the shared canvas or only receive. Collaborative drawing on a five-inch screen risks distracting from comprehension. Chose receive-focused with limited annotation — enough to highlight or point, not enough to redraw. Cost accepted: students couldn't show their working fluidly.

sections.caption: Whiteboard on mobile: receive-focused with limited annotation. Enough to follow the tutor's working, not enough to distract.

sections.heading: Decision 3 — India: UI fix or problem redefinition
sections.body: After the first India launch showed poor conversion, the choice was between iterating on the payment UI or stopping to research. Research revealed Indian students have no bank cards — the existing payment model was structurally unusable. Designed a parent payment link flow so students could request payment from a parent. Cost accepted: a second launch took longer.

sections.caption: Parent payment link flow — student requests payment from a parent, bypassing the card requirement entirely.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: Full live session experience shipped — voice/video call, shared whiteboard, LaTeX rendering, screenshare on student mobile. India v1 launched, then researched v2 with parent payment link, localised payment methods, exam preparation positioning, and low-end Android optimisation. Brainly Tutor reached 500,000 sessions within six months of product launch and 2 million by September 2022.

sections.caption: India onboarding — repositioned from homework help to exam preparation, optimised for low-end Android.

sections.text: The whiteboard and the call weren't features — they were the product's claim that this session was worth paying for.

experience.description: Leading product design for DailyFX, the world's most visited forex trading news and analysis portal. Responsible for the redesign of the core platform, establishing a shared design system, and mentoring a team of designers.
Designed core product features for the world's largest peer-to-peer learning community — 350M+ users globally. Led the design of live tutoring from concept through launch.
Contributed to the growth of PandaDoc's document automation platform. Focused on the document editor experience and workflow automation, improving conversion and retention.
Founded and scaled the design function at Storebox. Established the design system, brand identity, and created Europe's first fully digital self-storage customer experience.
Designed UI/UX for mobile games and interactive experiences. Built a strong foundation in user-centred design, visual communication, and real-time interface design under tight constraints.

philosophy.title: User-Centered Design
philosophy.description: Every design decision starts and ends with the user. I advocate for deep user research, empathy mapping, and continuous testing to ensure products genuinely serve people's needs — not just business assumptions.

philosophy.title: Iterative Approach
philosophy.description: Great design is never finished on the first pass. I embrace rapid prototyping and continuous iteration — shipping, learning, and refining based on real-world feedback rather than internal consensus.

philosophy.title: Interdisciplinary Collaboration
philosophy.description: Design thrives at intersections. I work closely with engineers, product managers, and business stakeholders to build solutions that are technically feasible, commercially viable, and delightful to use.

philosophy.title: Data-Driven Decisions
philosophy.description: Intuition is a starting point, not an endpoint. I combine qualitative insights with quantitative data to validate assumptions and measure the real impact of design on people and business outcomes.

about.headline: Pavel is a designer and leader, based in 🏰 Krakow, Poland.
about.bio: I'm a digital product designer and leader based in Krakow, Poland. With over a decade of experience designing digital products, I specialise in creating experiences that balance user needs with business goals — and in building the teams and systems that make great design repeatable.
about.bio2: I've had the privilege of working with fast-growing startups and established companies across fintech, edtech, and SaaS. I believe great design is invisible — it just works.
about.bio3: Outside of work I'm drawn to typography, film photography, and long trail runs in the mountains.
